final_answer:
Antibiotic resistance arises through the evolutionary process of natural selection. When bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, most are killed, but some may possess genetic mutations that confer resistance to the drug. These resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on their resistance traits to subsequent generations. Over time, this leads to the proliferation of antibiotic-resistant strains. 

The evolutionary mechanism involves selection pressure: antibiotics act as environmental stressors that eliminate susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to dominate. Resistance can also spread through horizontal gene transfer, where bacteria share resistance genes via plasmids or other genetic elements, accelerating the spread of resistance traits.  

Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process by increasing the frequency and duration of antibiotic exposure. Inappropriate use, such as incomplete courses or unnecessary prescriptions, allows bacteria to encounter sub-lethal concentrations of antibiotics. This environment favors the survival and proliferation of resistant strains, as non-resistant bacteria are selectively eliminated. Additionally, widespread use in agriculture and livestock further amplifies the selective pressure, promoting the emergence and dissemination of resistance genes across bacterial populations.
